lessons.title: What RAG actually is: the open-book exam
lessons.summary: Why a frozen model can't answer questions about your data, why fine-tuning is the wrong fix, and the two clocks (indexing time and query time) that every technique in this course runs on.

lessons.title: The pipeline end to end, and where it breaks
lessons.summary: RAG is five stages bolted together, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, generate, and end-to-end quality is the product of each stage's success rate, not the average. Today we trace the pipeline as a data flow and catalog the specific failure mode native to each stage.

lessons.title: Why text isn't searchable: strings to numbers
lessons.summary: Exact matching fails because people use different words for the same thing. The fix is to turn every chunk into a vector so similarity becomes arithmetic, which turns retrieval into a sparse storage problem with two very different layouts.

lessons.title: TF-IDF from scratch
lessons.summary: Two separate questions, how much a term matters here and whether it tells you anything at all, multiplied together. IDF is really surprisal, which is why it zeroes out stopwords without a stopword list.

lessons.title: Cosine similarity and why we normalize
lessons.summary: Ranking by dot product means a document concatenated to itself beats an exact match. Cosine fixes that by comparing direction and discarding magnitude, and normalizing at index time makes it cost a single multiply-accumulate.

lessons.title: Chunking 101: windows, overlap, the tradeoff
lessons.summary: The real reason to chunk is not context limits, it is that a long document's vector dilutes every term by about 1/sqrt(k). Overlap patches the boundary problem at a storage cost you can compute, and the famous 512 token default is folklore from BERT's architecture.

lessons.title: Tokens: what they are and what they cost
lessons.summary: BPE is a compression algorithm repurposed as a tokenizer, and the 4 chars per token rule breaks badly on code and non-Latin scripts. Tokenizers are model specific, and query-side context, not indexing, is what actually dominates a RAG bill.

lessons.title: Your first end-to-end RAG in 100 lines
lessons.summary: A complete retrieval pipeline with no dependencies, assembled from the last five days. Then two real failures traced to their exact cause: an off-topic query whose whole vector collapses to the word 'of', and a correct answer that ranks fourth because IDF measures rarity rather than meaning.

lessons.title: Neural embeddings: what the encoder adds
lessons.summary: Self-attention is a content addressable lookup with learned, soft matching, which is what gives one vector per word occurrence rather than per word type. It solves the vocabulary problem from Day 3, and costs quadratic attention, larger vectors, and all of your interpretability.

lessons.title: Pooling: mean, CLS, and why it matters
lessons.summary: Collapsing token vectors into one is lossy, and doing it without an attention mask makes your embeddings depend on batch composition. Raw CLS vectors score worse than averaged GloVe, and no pooling choice fixes anisotropy.

lessons.title: Contrastive training and InfoNCE
lessons.summary: InfoNCE is cross entropy over the passages in your batch, temperature decides which negatives your gradient actually pays attention to, and in-batch negatives give quadratic training signal for linear compute. The denominator is what fixes the anisotropy from Day 10.

lessons.title: Hard negatives, the biggest training lever
lessons.summary: Random negatives produce a loss around 240,000 times smaller than hard ones, so they stop teaching almost immediately. Mining harder negatives is the biggest quality lever available, and it is also how you accidentally train your model that correct answers are wrong.

lessons.title: Query and passage asymmetry, the silent bug
lessons.summary: Models handle the query/passage difference with separate encoders or a text prefix, and getting the prefix wrong fails without any error. I measured the cost on a 40 query benchmark and got 5 points of recall@1, with a confidence interval that crosses zero.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: build and measure a baseline
lessons.summary: Measured on a 40 query benchmark, dense retrieval beats the Day 8 TF-IDF system by 17.5 points of recall@1 with a confidence interval that does not cross zero. The win is not on the median query, it is that TF-IDF's failures land at rank 25 and rank 40 while the dense model's worst case is rank 5.

lessons.title: Exact kNN and why it doesn't scale
lessons.summary: Brute force search has an arithmetic intensity of 0.5 FLOPs per byte against a machine balance of 4, so it is memory bound by eight times and behaves like a table scan. Measured: 93 ms and 10.8 queries per second at a million vectors, exactly as the roofline predicts.

lessons.title: The recall, latency, memory triangle
lessons.summary: Recall in ANN means agreement with brute force, and the returns diminish hard: measured on real embeddings, scanning 1.7 percent of the data recovers 54 percent of the right answers and 13 percent recovers 95 percent. Which recall you need is a property of your whole pipeline, not your index.

lessons.title: HNSW I: small-world graphs, the intuition
lessons.summary: Greedy search on a pure nearest-neighbour graph gets 1.3 percent recall and stops after 1.7 hops, because every edge is short and local minima are everywhere. Eight random long edges per node more than double it, and HNSW is a skip list for metric space built on that idea.

lessons.title: HNSW II: M, efConstruction, efSearch
lessons.summary: Measured on a real incremental build: efSearch is a per-query knob you can change freely, while M and efConstruction are frozen at build time. Raising M past about 16 does nothing because the diversity heuristic refuses the extra edges, and a cheap efConstruction bakes a worse graph in permanently.

lessons.title: HNSW III: build one yourself
lessons.summary: Ninety lines of working HNSW, with layer sizes matching N/M^l exactly. Then a controlled comparison against the flat graph from Day 18 where the hierarchy contributed nothing at 2,800 vectors, which is a lesson about measuring at your own scale rather than trusting a paper's defaults.

lessons.title: IVF: clustering the vector space
lessons.summary: Measured: at 256 cells, nearly half of queries have their nearest neighbour in a cell they did not pick, which is why nprobe is a correctness requirement rather than a tuning knob. Compared at equal work rather than equal nprobe, finer partitions win decisively, and the sqrt(N) rule falls out of balancing the coarse scan against the list scan.

lessons.title: Product quantization I: the compression idea
lessons.summary: Splitting a vector into m pieces and quantizing each independently gives 256^m representable vectors from m bytes. Measured, PQ alone at 64x compression gets recall 0.646, but used as a shortlist with a full-vector rescoring pass it gets 0.992, which is why it is a filter rather than a replacement.

lessons.title: Product quantization II: asymmetric distance
lessons.summary: Precomputing an m by 256 table once per query turns scoring into table lookups and adds with no decode, and it is an exact reformulation rather than an approximation. Keeping the query unquantized is worth 17 points of recall over quantizing it, and the real win is 64 times less memory traffic.

lessons.title: IVF-PQ: billion scale on one machine
lessons.summary: Encoding the residual from the cell centroid rather than the raw vector is the idea that makes IVF-PQ work, and its value scales with how good your coarse quantizer is: measured, the gain triples going from 16 cells to 1024. The result is a billion vectors resident in 32 GB with the full data on SSD.
